title: Count out-of-order pairs
prompt:
A ranking list should be in ascending order of score. Measure how unsorted it is: return the number of pairs of positions i < j where scores[i] > scores[j]. Equal scores are not out of order.

- scores has 0 to 100,000 integers between 0 and 10^9.
- The answer can be as large as about 5 × 10^9, which still fits a JavaScript number exactly.
- Target O(n log n) time. Checking every pair is too slow for the largest inputs.
hints: Split the list in half. Every out-of-order pair is inside the left half, inside the right half, or crosses the middle.
Count the crossing pairs while merging the two sorted halves.
When a right-half value is taken before the remaining left-half values, each of those left values forms a pair with it: add len(left) − i.

solution.explanation: Merge sort returns both the sorted list and the count. Pairs inside each half are counted by the recursive calls. For pairs that cross the middle, both halves are sorted, so when the merge takes right[j] before left[i], every value from left[i] onwards is bigger and earlier. That adds len(left) − i pairs at once. Ties take the left value first, so equal scores never count.

complexity.notes: Counting adds O(1) work per merge step, so the cost is the same as merge sort. A Fenwick tree over compressed values is another O(n log n) approach.

followUps: Count only pairs where scores[i] > 2 × scores[j].
For each position, return how many later scores are smaller.
